synopsis: ACAS X succeeds TCAS but remains an advisory, pilot-in-the-loop system, making it a precedent for collision-warning logic rather than automatic braking [f1428, f15748]. Its threat-resolution validation relied primarily on encounter-model Monte Carlo simulations covering millions of encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours, alongside pilot assessment and retained flight evaluation [f1907, f1571, f1908, f1911]. This capability took years to build from radar-derived encounter models: European CREME drew on twelve million flights, while the MIT Lincoln Laboratory model used nine months of radar recordings; the booklet did not establish validation duration once that capability existed [f1909, f1430, f1433, f1910]. Acceptance came through RTCA, EUROCAE and aviation authorities, with minimum operational performance standards DO-385 and ED-256 published in October 2018 [f1434, f1429]. March 2022 committee minutes recorded European results suggesting ACAS Xa induced more near mid-air collisions than TCAS, a disparity MIT Lincoln Laboratory did not observe; sensor noise had not been assessed, leaving model representativeness in question and warning against reliance on one simulation toolchain [f1436, f1437, f1968, f1969]. For heavy off-road collision mitigation, the precedent supports statistical simulation as primary safety evidence only with substantial real-data foundations, motivating field-interaction logging on the existing warning fleet [f15756, f15757].
